Start here

Planned: 8 minutes: read the case and the policy now.

In this session you will work through one invented case in four short exercises, then answer ten questions. Exercise 5 is homework. The planned time is 90 minutes, with your instructor.

One idea runs through all of it: the assistant drafts; you check; you decide. An assistant is fast at producing a first draft. It is not responsible for what you send. You are.

  • Keep the case in view. You will compare answers with the e-mails and the policy all session. Use the printed case from your instructor, or open this page in a second window and keep that one on The case.
  • The assistant your employer allows, or none. If you have none, or are not allowed one, every exercise that needs an assistant's answer has one ready for you: one model's recorded answer (a model is the AI system behind an assistant). Two answers in exercise 3 are edited, and say so.
  • A practice tool, not an exam. The workbook carries its own answer key, so that it can check your answers on this computer with no server. Anyone who opens the page's files can read it. Nobody is graded.
  • Your answers stay here. What you type is kept in this browser, on this computer, and is sent nowhere. At the end, use Your answers to save a copy as a text file, or to clear everything.
  • The checks are helpers. Each Check button looks for simple signs and says what it found. It can miss things, and it can flag things that are fine. It points; you decide.
  • If this page will not work, open workbook-single-file.html, next to this folder: the same workbook in one file. The case is also in the case folder as plain files you can open or print.
  • Nothing here is real. The businesses, the people and the figures are invented. Never paste real customer or company data into this workbook.

The case

You are (invented), in customer service at (invented), a small wholesale supplier of cups, lids and packaging to cafes and bakeries, with about a dozen staff. One of your customers, of (invented), has had a late, short and partly damaged delivery, and she is not happy.

Everything the exercises need is below. Read the thread and the policy now; you will come back to them in every exercise.

Two words in the thread: a cash-and-carry is a wholesale shop where a business pays at the till and takes the goods away itself; 12 oz is the size of the cups, twelve fluid ounces, about 350 ml.

The e-mail thread: five messages over nine days

Exercise 1: From a wish to a brief

  
Planned: 18 minutes. You practise writing a request as a five-part brief.

  
Goal: turn a one-line wish into a brief that an assistant can act on. A brief is a request in five parts that gives the assistant everything it needs: the situation, the material (the text it works from), the task, the form of the answer, and the limits.


  
Step 1: See what a wish produces

  
A colleague pasted the whole thread into an assistant, with one line above it:  Below is what came back. It is polished and polite. Read it as if you were about to press Send, with the thread and the policy open beside it.

  

  

  
Write a short list, one line for each problem you find:

  
    
    
  • anything the reply decides or promises that nobody asked it to;
    • 
    
  • anything it says happened that the thread does not show;
    • 
    
  • anything that stops you sending it as it is.
    • 
  

  
  
  
Then press the first button to compare your list with the instructor's, and the second to see what the automatic checker finds. The checker reads figures and some promise words; expect it to miss most of what is wrong here.

  

    
    
  

  

  


  
Step 2: Write the request again, in five parts

  
Write each part as if to a capable new colleague who has never heard of this customer, and who will fill any gap you leave with a guess.


  

    
    
Who you are (, in customer service), who the reader is (), what has happened, and why it matters today.

    
  

  

    
    
The material is the text the assistant works from. Press the button to put the whole thread in this box; do not type a note in its place. Then press Add the policy: your limits will rely on it, and the assistant cannot follow a rule it has not been given.

    

      
      
    

    
  

  

    
    
The one job, starting with a verb: draft, summarise, list.

    
  

  

    
    
How long, in what shape, in what tone. For example: "at most 150 words, in three short paragraphs, plain text".

    
  

  

    
    
What the answer must not do. Write at least one sentence that starts with "Do not".

    
  

  

    
  

  


  
Step 3, if you have an assistant: try your brief (skip it if you are short of time)

  
Copy your brief as one text, send it, and paste the reply here. Check it, and compare it with the reply in step 1. What changed, and why?

  

    
    
  

  
  
  

    
  

  


  

    Compare with one strong brief: for reading afterwards
    
Open this after you have written and checked your own brief, not before. It is one way to write it. Yours can differ and still be strong: what matters is that each part does its job.

    

  







  
Exercise 2: Summarise, and prove it

  
Planned: 20 minutes. You practise asking for an answer that can be checked, and checking it.

  
Goal: ask for a summary you can check, then check its figures and facts against the thread.


  
Step 1: Make the request checkable

  
Your manager, , has to decide today on the customer's request for a credit. This request for a summary is almost ready. Add one line to its Form part, the part of a brief that says how long the answer should be and in what shape. To find it, scroll down past the thread: Form is the part just above Limits, which is the last part. Each part starts on a line of its own, such as "## Form": the ## only marks where a part begins. Your line asks the assistant to say, after each fact, which message the fact comes from. That one line turns checking from a search into a glance. Then press Check my request.

  
  
  

    
    
    
  

  


  
Step 2: Get an answer, and check it

  
Send your request to your assistant and paste its answer below. No assistant, or not allowed one? Use the recorded answer: one assistant's answer to this request, made with this line in its Form part: 

  

    
  

  

  
  
  

    
  

  


  
Step 3: Read, decide, and correct

  
For each Look again, open the thread and decide: keep it, fix it, or take it out. Then pick the three bullets you trust least and read each one against the message it cites, word by word: a sentence can pass every check and still say the opposite of the thread.

  
Write one line for each of the three: the bullet's number, then "agrees", or "differs:" and what the message really says. For example: "4: differs: message 3 says ...". This box is for you; it is not checked.

  
  
  
Last, if you have time, write the version you would really send; otherwise finish it after the session. In at most  words (message numbers in brackets are not counted), it must say:

  
    
    
  • the order number and the invoice number;
    • 
    
  • what went wrong: that the order came late, that cartons were missing, and that cartons arrived damaged;
    • 
    
  • the amount in question: the credit of  that  asks for, or its two parts;
    • 
    
  • what was promised, including that 's promise to confirm a delivery day by  was not kept, and that no credit was promised.
    • 
  

  
The check looks for words, not meaning: for example late, missing, damaged, promised, Friday, did not. A due date followed by a later delivery date also counts as late. It does not count a word after "not" or "nothing".

  
If you want a frame to start from, fill in this one, with the message numbers in brackets:

  
- Order ... and invoice ... (msg ...).
- What went wrong: due ..., delivered late on ...; ... cartons missing; ... arrived crushed (msg ...).
- What we promised: ...; not kept: ... (msg ...). No credit was promised (msg ...).
- Amount in question: ... (msg ...).
- Your decision: ...

  
  
  

    
  

  

  
What the check reads: every figure written in digits, compared as a number, so 1,250.00 and 1250 are the same figure. A date written as 28/02 is compared by its day and month. Message numbers in brackets, such as (msg 3), are read as citations, not as figures. A figure written in words, such as "six", is not checked.







  
Exercise 3: Find what is wrong

  
Planned: 15 minutes. You practise naming what is wrong in an answer that looks right.

  
Goal: find the errors in replies that read well.

  
In the session: answers A and B, eleven sentences. Answer C, further down, is for those who finish early, or homework.

  
Here are replies to 's last message, answering the strong brief of exercise 1. Answer A is one assistant's recorded reply, unchanged, with the assistant's own notes under it. Answer B is the same reply, edited to plant errors that A does not contain. The assistant's notes are not numbered, but read them. Keep the thread and the policy open. For each numbered sentence, choose one mark:

  
    
    
  • Fine: true to the thread, and allowed by the policy.
    • 
    
  • A wrong figure: a number that is wrong, or used with the wrong meaning.
    • 
    
  • Not in the material: a fact that is in neither the thread nor the policy.
    • 
    
  • Against the policy: a promise or an offer the policy does not allow.
    • 
  

  
Some sentences can be marked two ways. Pick the mark you can defend; the result says when the key accepts both.

  
Where the hard ones hide: compare what answer A says was sent with messages 4 and 5, and check every day and date it gives against the thread.

  

    The request behind the replies
    

  

  

  

    
  

  


  
Then: what does a machine catch?

  
Run the automatic reply check on answers A and B, and compare what it finds with what you found.

  

  

  
  






  
Exercise 4: What must not go in

  
Planned: 20 minutes. You practise deciding what must not be pasted into a public assistant, and preparing a table so that it can be.

  
Goal: sort what may be pasted, and prepare a table so that nothing personal leaves this computer.

  
Your employer's own policy on AI tools comes first. If it is stricter than anything in this exercise, follow it.


  
Part 1: Sort the eight snippets

  
For each snippet, choose a pile:

  
    
    
  • Fine to paste: already public, or written to be published, even if it is not public yet, and holding nothing about a person.
    • 
    
  • Paste after removing details: the question does not need the names, contacts or other details that point to a person or a customer; take them out first.
    • 
    
  • Do not paste: what is left would still harm someone or break a promise of confidence, or nothing useful is left once the details are out.
    • 
  

  
Think about who could be harmed, and whether the question needs the detail at all. Some snippets can go in two piles; pick the one you can defend.

  

  

    
  

  


  
Part 2: Prepare the orders table

  
Your manager asks:  You want an assistant to work it out from the orders table (in The case). Three words you will need:

  
    
    
  • Stand-in: a made-up label used instead of a real value, such as Customer 01 instead of a business name.
    • 
    
  • Key: the list of which stand-in means which real value. It stays on this computer; you never paste it.
    • 
    
  • Map back: put the real values back into the assistant's answer, using the key.
    • 
  

  
For example: in the extract,  becomes Customer 01. The key says Customer 01 is . When the assistant's answer mentions Customer 01, this page puts  back. The helper runs only in this browser.

  
    
    
  1. For each column, choose: keep it, replace each value with a stand-in, or leave it out. Keep only what the question needs.
    2. 
    
  2. Press Prepare the extract. Read the text and the question under it, then press Check what I am about to paste.
    3. 
    
  3. Paste the extract into your assistant. Paste its answer in the last box, and press Put the real names back. No assistant? Press No assistant? Use an example answer under the last box: it puts in an answer that uses your stand-ins, and then Put the real names back works the same way.
    4.

Exercise 5: Make it reusable

  
Homework, about eight minutes. You practise turning a request that worked into a template a colleague can reuse.

  
Goal: turn the request of exercise 2 into a template a colleague can fill in for any customer.

  
    
    
  1. Put the exercise 2 request in the box below.
    2. 
    
  2. Replace everything that belongs to this case with a named placeholder in square brackets, such as [CUSTOMER NAME]. The whole thread becomes one placeholder, such as [PASTE THE E-MAIL THREAD HERE].
    3. 
    
  3. Keep what is true every time: the form and the limits.
    4. 
    
  4. Add one line at the top for your colleague. For example: "Fill in every part in square brackets, then send. Afterwards, check every figure against the message it names."

The ten-question check

  
Planned: 9 minutes, with the close.

  
Ten questions, two for each of the five skills. The last two are about templates, which exercise 5 practises as homework: answer them now as a preview, or after the homework. Choose the best answer to each, then check. Every option has an explanation, so a wrong choice still teaches you something.
